name: Testosterone / TRT for beard

lead: Beard growth begins at puberty and is driven by androgens, mainly dihydrotestosterone (DHT) made from testosterone. Some people in looksmaxxing communities therefore discuss testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) as a route to a fuller beard.

Testosterone is a prescription medication used chiefly for hypogonadism and gender-affirming care. It is not approved for cosmetic beard growth, and no trials were found that test it for that purpose in men with normal levels.

paras: Testosterone is converted in hair follicles to DHT, which stimulates facial hair follicles; beard growth rate is also described as largely genetic.

Documented effects of exogenous testosterone include acne, fluid retention, gynecomastia, raised hematocrit, suppressed sperm production, worsened sleep apnea and, for scalp hair, possible androgenetic hair loss. It is a controlled substance in many jurisdictions (Schedule III in the US) and contraindicated in pregnancy.

lead: Testosterone is an androgen hormone used as a medication, principally for male hypogonadism, and also in gender-affirming therapy.[1] Its virilizing effects include growth of facial and body hair.[1] Beard development begins at puberty and is stimulated by dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is made from testosterone.[2]

In looksmaxxing discussions, testosterone replacement therapy is sometimes raised as a way to increase beard density. Reference sources describe the hormonal mechanism but report that the rate of beard growth is largely genetic.[2] The same sources document adverse effects and legal controls on testosterone.[1]

paras: In skin and hair follicles, testosterone is converted to the more potent androgen DHT, which contributes to virilizing effects including facial and body hair.[1][2] DHT also contributes to scalp hair loss in people predisposed to it.[2] Drugs that block 5-alpha reductase, such as finasteride, can reduce androgenic effects but may also reduce facial and body hair growth.[1]

Reported effects include acne, oily skin, scalp hair loss, swelling, gynecomastia, mood changes, increased aggression and increased sex drive.[1] Exogenous testosterone can suppress sperm production, sometimes causing reversible infertility, and may raise hematocrit, worsen sleep apnea and enlarge the prostate.[1] In February 2025 the FDA removed language on increased cardiovascular risk from the boxed warning while adding a warning about increased blood pressure.[1] Testosterone is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1]

Testosterone was first isolated in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939.[1] It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, Schedule IV in Canada and Class C in the UK, and is banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[1]

No studies found that test testosterone for cosmetic beard growth in men with normal levels. Testosterone's virilizing effects on facial hair are described in general references on the medication, and studies of facial hair outcomes in transgender men are a separate population.[1]

lore.intro: Beard-growth discussions in appearance communities often mention androgen levels as a determinant of facial hair; this entry summarizes that belief alongside published reference descriptions.

claims.claim: Raising testosterone will make a beard grow fuller.
TRT is a low-risk way to improve appearance.

timeline.event: US Anabolic Steroid Control Act designates anabolic steroids as controlled substances.[1]
